national.title: L3Harris struggled to find location of outage during ground stop
national.summary: It took several hours for contractor L3Harris to pinpoint the source of an outage that caused last Friday's nationwide ground stop​.
national.body: The contractor that owns the network running the nation's air traffic control system took several hours to pinpoint the source of an outage that caused Friday's nationwide ground stop, forcing a delay in lifting it, according to a person familiar with the investigation. L3Harris' network operations center is located in Melbourne, Florida, and provides real-time updates to network outages in the ATC system. On Friday, however, sources say the company was not immediately able to identify the IP address where the issue was originating. Where the outage had occurred should have been immediately apparent, given the sophistication of the system that tracks outages, another source said.The FAA's Federal Telecommunications Infrastructure network, known as FTI, became unstable as data flooded the network, attempting to connect 1,000 times every 4 to 5 seconds, the FAA said. This resulted in a disruption of the system and "instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds."The FAA's initial investigation identified two possible sources, one in Amarillo, Texas, and the other in El Dorado, Arkansas. The agency and L3Harris ultimately concluded that the Arkansas site, where a new router was being deployed, had caused the outage.Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told reporters on Tuesday that L3Harris needs to perform better amid concerns about its ability to monitor the network. "They didn't identify and isolate. That concerns me," Duffy said on Capitol Hill Tuesday. L3Harris says that its network operations center is monitored 24/7 to identify latency issues and outages. The company referred CBS News to its statement from Saturday afternoon, in response to inquiries.In that statement, L3Harris said it has worked "in close coordination with the FAA" on modernizing the National Airspace System and has completed more than 70% of the conversion from legacy copper wires to fiber optics.The company said it supports the FAA's investigation into the conditions that caused the nationwide ground stop.

national.title: "No indication" outages are related to cyberattacks, officials say
national.summary: Officials are testifying at a House committee hearing on worldwide threats as a series of network outages, including Microsoft Outlook and several banking institutions, have rattled Americans.
national.body: Washington — Top U.S. national security officials told Congress they have found no evidence that a string of technology outages affecting airlines, banks, Microsoft services and national security communications systems were connected or caused by malicious cyberattacks, even as lawmakers pressed for answers about an outage at the National Security Agency and reports of potential Iranian attacks on U.S. soil.At Wednesday's House Homeland Security Committee hearing, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia attempted to reassure lawmakers that federal agencies were investigating the disruptions and monitoring possible threats."We have seen nothing that would indicate that they are related," Mullin said, adding that DHS had contacted private industry while reviewing the outages.Mullin said later in the hearing that he is "98% confident" that recent outages are not the result of malicious activity from foreign adversaries, but did admit that he had "absolutely not" seen this many outages in this amount of time.Clayton said intelligence officials had reached a similar assessment after reviewing the incidents with government agencies and cybersecurity experts in the private sector."These are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack," Clayton said.Raia said FBI cybersecurity specialists had been involved in examining the incidents from the beginning."At this point, there is no indication whatsoever that there is any cyber malicious activity related to any of those incidents," Raia said. national.summary: America's Persian Gulf allies and oil tankers are under fire as Iran appears to lash out following U.S. strikes on a key island in the Strait of Hormuz.
national.body: The U.S. Treasury has targeted funding for the Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group in its latest round of sanctions tied to Operation Economic Outcast. One of the targets of the sanctions was the Wa Ta'awanu Association, which the U.S. said is a charity that "provides cover for Hizballah's activities under the guise of delivering humanitarian services." "The Iranian regime's attempts to infringe on Lebanon's sovereignty through terror proxies like Hizballah will not be tolerated," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. "The U.S. government will continue to disrupt Iran's attempts to exert influence in the region and fund its proxies." The sanctions also targeted an alleged gold and cash smuggling network run by Hezbollah and the IRGC's Quds Force. The Hezbollah militant group has been fighting Israel in southern Lebanon for years, but the latest round of violence was sparked in the wake of the U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran in February. In solidarity, Hezbollah began targeting northern Israel with missile and drone launches, prompting an invasion by Israel.

national.title: As overdose deaths fall, White House makes misleading claims about who deserves credit
national.summary: In a statement celebrating the historic drop in drug deaths, the White House pointed to successes since President Trump took office. In fact, the biggest progress happened under the Biden administration.
national.body:
Families look on as President Donald Trump speaks during a ceremony to sign the "Halt All Lethal Trafficking of Fentanyl Act" in the East Room of the White House on July 16, 2025. Evan Vucci/AP hide caption

When the White House announced big improvements in the number of people dying from fatal drug overdoses earlier this week, officials pointed to hopeful new data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention showing U.S. drug deaths have plunged to their lowest level in roughly a decade, saving nearly 50,000 lives each year.

Health NPR Exclusive: U.S. overdose deaths plummet, saving thousands of lives But leading drug policy researchers say the White House statement also made misleading claims about the timing and cause of the remarkable public health success when it said that gains occurred primarily over the last 18 months due to policies enacted under President Trump's leadership.

"The historic decline in drug overdose deaths demonstrates that America is unequivocally winning the fight against illicit drugs," White House Office of National Drug Control Policy director Sara Carter said in a statement .

Carter credited heightened border security under Trump and claims of success dismantling "narco-terrorist" organizations for the recovery. "Critically, this represents a an approximately 41.5% decrease in total drug overdose deaths compared to the peak under the previous administration," the statement said.

What the White House failed to disclose is that declines in overdose fatalities began much earlier, under the Biden administration, with most of the gains occurring before Trump returned to office.

"Since the spring of 2023, we have seen a steady decline in overdose deaths," said Vanda Felbab-Brown, a drug policy expert at the Brookings Institution. "The fact that it has been sustained is very important."

According to CDC data, reductions in drug deaths began in 2023 and have continued steadily for at least 39 consecutive months — not 18 months as the ONDCP statement said. By the time Biden left office, fatal overdoses had already dropped by roughly one-third, an improvement described by addiction experts at the time as unprecedented.

national.title: Hegseth meets with Venezuelan interim leaders in latest Trump Cabinet visit since Maduro's ouster
national.summary: Secretary Pete Hegseth's visit comes at a time of uncertainty for Venezuelans regarding who will lead the nation in the coming months and years.
national.body:
Regina Garcia Cano, Associated Press Regina Garcia Cano, Associated Press

CARACAS, Venezuela (AP) — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is visiting Venezuela to meet with interim authorities on Wednesday, underscoring efforts by President Donald Trump's administration to deepen its influence in the South American country since U.S. forces ousted then-President Nicolás Maduro in January.

Hegseth is the latest member of Trump's Cabinet to travel to Venezuela following visits this year by the Interior and Energy secretaries, who have focused on efforts to tap its oil reserves and critical minerals. Trump said in August that Hegseth helped broker a sweeping deal for the U.S. to take control of some Venezuelan oil reserves.

WATCH: Trump says Venezuela sent him 1 million barrels of oil as a 'gift'

Venezuelan state television broadcast footage of Hegseth at the presidential palace in Caracas, alongside acting President Delcy Rodríguez. Hegseth, whose visit was not publicly announced by the Pentagon, is there months after American forces carried out a surprise nighttime raid in the Venezuelan capital to capture Maduro and whisk him to New York to face drug trafficking charges. Maduro has denied the accusations in U.S. court.

Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News

The head of U.S. military operations in Latin America, Gen. Francis Donovan of U.S. Southern Command, also has met interim authorities at least twice in Venezuela this year.

The U.S. military has been expanding its attention on the region since Trump returned to the White House last year, with the Republican president promising to focus more on the Western Hemisphere and battle Latin American drug cartels.

national.title: Largest U.S. data centers use as much power as some countries
national.summary: Hyperscale data centers used almost 2% of all U.S. electricity between 2024 and 2025, a Harvard study shows.
national.body: The largest data centers in the U.S. collectively consume roughly as much energy as some individual states and even some countries, according to new research from Harvard University.Researchers found that so-called hyperscale data centers, which occupy as much space as several football fields, consumed 82 terawatt-hours of electricity, or 1.8% of all U.S. electricity, between 2024 and 2025. That's roughly the equivalent of what a state like Missouri uses or a nation like Denmark. Their total carbon emissions were approximately 26 metric tons of carbon dioxide. Harvard scientist Gianluca Guidi, the lead author of the paper published in Nature Sustainability this week, told CBS News that it took two years to analyze the electricity use and carbon dioxide emissions of 403 hyperscale data centers between May 2024 and April 2025. He added that their estimated energy consumption is likely understated, given the swift pace of the AI buildout across the U.S."The data stops in April 2025, which in AI time is basically ancient history," Guidi said. There are now more than double that number of large-scale facilities operating in the U.S., with an additional 2,000 planned or under development. "The industry is growing faster than anyone can track it," Guidi added. The study highlights AI's dependence on data centers as well as their outsized impact on the environment. Guidi explained why the facilities are such heavy electricity users. "Every email you send, every photo you post, every show you stream, every question you ask of any generative AI software goes through a building like this," he said of the windowless facilities housing tens of thousands of computers that run around the clock. The machines generate a lot of heat and require constant cooling. "So it's basically a factory that never sleeps," Guidi said.While he's excited about AI's capabilities and considers himself an industry proponent, Guidi called for more consideration of when and how facilities are built."The evidence shouldn't show up after the buildings do, and neither should the public's voice," he said. national.title: William and Kate reflect on 'enduring' UK-India ties with Modi
national.summary: The meeting in New Delhi was a late addition to the royal couple's India visit, which has also included their appearance at the annual Earthshot Prize
national.body:
The Prince and Princess of Wales have met with Prime Minister Narendra Modi to reflect on the enduring ties between the UK and India, as they wrapped up their three-day visit to the country.

William and Catherine arrived in New Delhi on Wednesday for the final leg of their first official overseas trip together in four years.

The meeting was a late addition to the couple's schedule and came after Modi confirmed he would be back from a scheduled trip to the Philippines in time to see the royals.

It comes a day after the royal couple were in Mumbai for the annual Earthshot Prize, which was founded by the prince and remains one of his biggest personal projects.

Street cricket with a legend then metro ride as William and Kate begin India visit

Published 2 days ago A Kensington Palace spokesperson said the royals and Modi discussed the "strength and importance of the UK–India bilateral relationship, reflecting on the deep and enduring ties between the two countries and the opportunities to strengthen their partnership in the years ahead".

The prince and princess also spoke "warmly" of their time in the country, thanking the prime minister and the people for their welcome, and added how much they enjoyed returning to India, a decade after their last visit.

Modi called it a "pleasure" to meet them, and said he looks forward to "further strengthening" the India-UK partnership for the "shared prosperity of the people of our nations and the wider world".

Tens of millions of people globally are expected to pick up their joysticks as Rockstar Games, the company behind the series, rolls out GTA 6 on Nov. 19 in countries around the world. national.summary: Five months after a fire at a food storage warehouse rocked Boyle Heights and East Los Angeles, residents say they still feel the effects on their health and are demanding transparency.
national.body: Five months after a fire at a food storage warehouse rocked Boyle Heights and East Los Angeles, residents say they still feel the effects on their health and are demanding transparency.One community nonprofit, California Communities Against Toxics, has filed lawsuits against the Environmental Protection Agency, seeking air quality monitoring and other testing data taken after the fire broke out. "My back hurts, because my lungs were damaged and I was coughing up blood," East LA resident Sofia Quiñones said. Residents like Karen Noga of Boyle Heights say they have developed symptoms since the fire began in mid-June. national.title: Jeffries wins Democratic nomination for House speaker
national.summary: Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries easily won his party's nomination for the next speaker of the House on Wednesday.
national.body: Washington — Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries easily won his party's nomination for the next speaker of the House on Wednesday, paving the way for his election when Democrats take control of the chamber in January.Jeffries' current and incoming Democratic colleagues voted 251 to 11 to back his nomination for the gavel during a closed-door meeting where members were also choosing the rest of the House Democratic leadership. The caucus also voted to elevate Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts as the next majority leader, the first woman to hold that position.The speaker is ultimately elected by the full House chamber, a vote that will occur at the beginning of the new Congress. With Democrats on track to control more than 250 seats, Jeffries' path to gaining the 218 votes needed for the speakership is all but secured. Jeffries would be the first Black House speaker in U.S. history. The New York Democrat faced some hesitance from new progressive members heading into Wednesday's leadership vote. Seven incoming progressives who voted against him said in a statement that they were hoping to secure policy commitments from Jeffries on a number of fronts."Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues. We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations," the new members said. "While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership."The members who released the statement were Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York, Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, Frederick Haynes of Texas, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Donavan McKinney of Michigan, Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania and Claire Valdez of New York.But no other Democrat put their name forward to directly challenge Jeffries' bid. national.title: Democrats nominate Hakeem Jeffries to be US Speaker of the House
national.summary: The nomination sets him on the path to become the first black lawmaker to lead the chamber when Democrats take control of the House in January.
national.body:
Democrats in the US House of Representatives officially nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be Speaker, setting him on the path to become the first black lawmaker to lead the chamber.

The House will elect its new Speaker on 3 January, when the next term begins and Democrats will be in the majority.

His election to the powerful position - the Speaker is in line to succeed the president after the vice-president - is widely expected. Should he win, Jeffries will preside over his party's largest House majority in years and benefit from the Senate also being under Democrats' control.

Jeffries told reporters after the vote that the nomination was "a high honour and a distinct privilege".

As of Wednesday, Democrats will hold at least 257 seats in the House next year, which is well beyond the 218 needed for a majority. Seven races from the recent midterm elections are still uncalled.

Jeffries, who represents a district in New York, was re-elected as the party leader in a 251-11 closed-door vote on Wednesday. He has served as minority leader since 2023.

Despite overwhelming support in Wednesday's vote, Jeffries faced a handful of holdouts from new members in the party's left wing, who have said the party's sweeping victory in the midterm elections is a sign voters want change.

"While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes in this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of our leadership," seven incoming lawmakers, including fellow New Yorkers Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, said in a statement.

national.title: Grand Theft Auto 6 is a masterpiece, say critics
national.summary: Critics have their say as to whether GTA 6, the most anticipated video game of all time, lives up to the hype.
national.body:
After 13 years of waiting, record-breaking trailers and lengthy delays, critics have given their answer to one of the year's biggest questions.

Does Grand Theft Auto 6, surely the most anticipated game of all time, live up to the hype?

Metacritic, which aggregates reviews from critics, averages it at 99 out of 100 , external - tying with Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which has held the record since 1998.

Reviewers overwhelmingly agreed the open-world action game was an ambitious, ground-breaking title that was well worth the wait.

Not everyone is enjoying the glowing praise - with some posters to online forums objecting to what one called "the ultra fan-boy hype."

But there is no question the reviewers have been effusive with their praise, with gaming website IGN , external branding GTA 6 "unprecedented", "unbelievable" and "unmissable".

Meanwhile in its five star review, Eurogamer said makers Rockstar had "pushed back the horizon of video games once again" with its graphics, storytelling and world building.

"The awe is all part of the point, of course, and GTA 6 is nothing if not truly awesome," reviewer Chris Tapsell wrote , external , but he added "there are also nits to pick".

national.summary: Anthropic's stock is poised to start trading on Nasdaq Thursday in one of the largest IPOs of all time. The AI world is watching.
national.body: Anthropic's blockbuster initial public offering is set to launch on Thursday, a milestone that will test investor enthusiasm for the company behind the popular Claude chatbot and the burgeoning artificial intelligence sector."This is a case where the deal is so large and important, so central to the AI thesis, that it's going to be a turning point for the AI sector," Matthew Kennedy, a senior market strategist at investment bank Renaissance Capital, told CBS News. "Even non-AI companies are going to feel the ripple effects, especially in the IPO market."Anthropic shares are scheduled to start trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker symbol "ANT" after markets open Thursday at 9:30 a.m. EST. What the stock price will tell usIn its most recent regulatory filing, San Francisco-based Anthropic said it will offer 825 million shares priced at between $70 and $78, which is expected to raise up to $64.3 billion. Sources tell CBS News that Anthropic may price shares at the high end of the range or even above $80 because of strong demand for its shares. It will formally set its final IPO price on Wednesday night, the sources said.The company also plans to raise an additional $26 billion from a slate of other companies, including chipmaker AMD, chip infrastructure provider Broadcom, Google, Microsoft and Nvidia, all of which have a stake in the AI race.The market debut is expected to value Anthropic at up to $1.4 trillion, short of the $2 trillion valuation that some IPO experts projected earlier this year. Still, the AI developer — which launched only in 2021 — is on track to stage what could become the second-largest IPO ever. national.summary: Five European nations have reached an agreement with Rwanda to deport failed asylum seekers to the African nation, but it's far from a done deal.
national.body: London — Five European Union countries have announced a plan to establish a deportation center in Rwanda next year to which they hope to send migrants whose asylum requests they have rejected.The plan has echoes of President Trump's controversial initiative to deport migrants to third countries to which they have no links, and an effort by a previous British government that failed to clear legal hurdles. It is an attempt by the five European nations to address widespread concerns about mass-migration that have fueled political change across the continent, but it is far from guaranteed to succeed, or even to get off the ground.Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands have reached an agreement in principle with Rwanda to open a so-called "return hub" in the landlocked African nation in 2027. Unlike the U.S. program, the plan would only apply to migrants who have exhausted all legal avenues to remain in Europe and subsequently been placed under a deportation order.Rather than being returned to their countries of origin, some migrants would instead be transferred to Rwanda, where they would have the option of staying or returning to their home countries. The plan is intended to provide the European nations an alternative for cases in which deportation to a migrant's country of origin is not possible, either because those countries will not accept them, or due to circumstances that could endanger the migrant if they return.Many European governments have sought to reduce the number of migrants entering their countries, or already present without permission, in the face of mounting political pressure from voters. As an example of the kind of statistics fueling that public concern, there were some 230,000 foreign nationals in Germany at the end of 2025 who were legally required to leave the country, according to the Die Welt newspaper, yet government figures show fewer than 23,000 deportations were carried out during the year."If people without the right to remain in the EU cannot be removed from the country, our entire asylum system becomes absurd," Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said this week. "If the state sets limits, then these must be respected."According to a statement from the Netherlands government, migrants deported to Rwanda under the proposed program would initially be accommodated in an "open, temporary facility." national.title: 'Grand Theft Auto VI' arrives with enormous hype and expectations after 13-year wait
national.summary: After a 13-year wait, one of entertainment's biggest releases is finally here.
national.body:
Jonathan Landrum Jr., Associated Press Jonathan Landrum Jr., Associated Press

LOS ANGELES (AP) — After a 13-year wait, one of entertainment's biggest releases is finally here.

"Grand Theft Auto VI" launches Thursday, sending players back to Vice City and testing whether Rockstar Games can follow one of the bestselling video games ever made with another cultural and commercial phenomenon.

The latest installment becomes playable at midnight local time on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X'S, meaning players in Asia and other regions can start playing hours before its U.S. release.

New Zealand was among the first countries where players could access the game, and internet providers prepared for a surge in downloads as midnight approached.

"The game file size at 212 gigabytes is unprecedented," said Kurt Rodgers, network strategy manager for Chorus New Zealand. "That's more than a quarter of the average household's data usage in an entire month, all in one go."

In the capital, Wellington, players stayed up to be among the first to try "Grand Theft Auto VI."

Among them was Adam Simmons, 50, a director of photography who launched the game in his living room as soon as it unlocked, keeping the volume low to avoid waking his wife and daughters.

national.title: 'The drones don't fly here' - BBC reports from Ukraine's new front line
national.summary: Ukrainian forces are fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet tunnel in the Kharkiv region.
national.body:
There's a new front in the war in Ukraine, and it is underground.

For the past seven months Ukrainian forces have been living and fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet gas pipeline in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.

With a diameter of just over a metre there is enough room only to crawl. But it is relatively safe from the drones that now saturate the skies above the front line – and make it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance.

Going underground is now the "only option", says Zanuda, who has helped plan Ukraine's tunnel operation and calls it a new world of fighting. But, he acknowledges, it is hard.

"On the surface you always have some room to manoeuvre, but here you can only engage the enemy head-on."

The journey to get to this subterranean battleground in the Kharkiv region only reinforced the dangers on the ground: a high-speed move by vehicle across open fields, followed by a long march across muddy ground – accompanied by Ukrainian troops with their weapons loaded, ready to shoot down Russian drones.

Arriving at the tunnel entrance, the first thing to hit you is the lingering smell of gas and fetid air.

Both sides use openings in the pipeline to get to the surface, where most of the fighting takes place. They have made breaches in the ground, and used welding tools to break through the thick steel.

national.title: Trump plans to meet separately with Putin on his China trip in addition to their 3-way talks with Xi
national.summary: President Donald Trump plans to meet separately with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday in China, in addition to their already scheduled three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, a U.S. official confirmed.
national.body:
Michelle L. Price, Associated Press Michelle L. Price, Associated Press

SHENZHEN, China (AP) — President Donald Trump plans to meet separately with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday in China, in addition to their already scheduled three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, a U.S. official confirmed.

Trump's meeting with Putin would be the first time that the leaders have held talks since their discussions in Alaska last year that failed to broker a deal to ease Russia's war in Ukraine.

Trump has frequently boasted of his rapport with Putin as relations between the United States and Ukraine appear to have cratered recently. Trump rejected new Russia sanctions while Kyiv was undermined by disruptions in satellite support for its drones during the war.

Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News

The U.S. official who confirmed the Trump-Putin meeting in China spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity to share plans that were not yet public.

The exact timing of the meeting on Thursday was unclear. Trump already had public plans for a separate meeting with Xi and a historic trilateral meeting with Xi and Putin.

Trump said he plans to talk with Xi and Putin in their joint meeting about limiting nuclear weapons and bringing an end to the war in Ukraine, which began in 2022 with Russia's invasion. Analysts are not expecting substantive breakthroughs despite the unprecedented nature of the meeting.

national.title: Julio Iglesias facing court investigation over alleged sexual offences
national.summary: The 83-year-old singer is accused of abusing two former employees at Caribbean residences in 2021.
national.body:
Singer Julio Iglesias is facing an investigation by Spain's national court over allegations he sexually abused and assaulted two female former staff members

Two women, who worked for the 83-year-old in the Caribbean, have accused him of abuse which they say took place in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic in 2021.

The announcement comes after Spanish prosecutors dropped an inquiry into the claims earlier this year after concluding that they lacked jurisdiction because the alleged crimes took place abroad.

Iglesias, who has been a household name in Spain since the 1960s and has sold millions of records worldwide, has previously denied the allegations .

But in a statement published on Wednesday , external (in Spanish), national court Judge Antonio Piña said the account given in the complaint, alongside preliminary evidence provided, justified opening criminal proceedings.

He added that the investigation would cover parts of the complaint relating to potential crimes against sexual freedom, as well as assault and degrading treatment.

But the court will not investigate claims made in the lawsuit of human trafficking or crimes against workers' rights. Piña said these allegations were dismissed after he looked into the hiring of the women and found there was "no deception or artifice involved".

Piña said the former employees had been summoned to testify in person on 3 February.

national.title: Trump shakes hands with Putin and Xi ahead of historic talks in China
national.summary: The three leaders will meet together for the first time on Thursday during a closely-watched summit.
national.body:
Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin met for the first time in more than a year on Wednesday, as they prepared for landmark talks in China with Xi Jinping.

The US president was greeted off his plane by the Chinese leader as he arrived in Shenzhen for a summit of Asia-Pacific leaders, which will culminate in a closely-watched meeting between the pair and the Russian president.

After a carefully choreographed handshake and hug between Trump and Xi on the tarmac, the US president later greeted and exchanged pleasantries with Putin ahead of a reception.

Trump and Putin are expected to hold one-on-one talks on the sidelines of the summit on Thursday, in which the war in Ukraine could be discussed.

However the main focus during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum (Apec) will be on the US-China-Russia talks on Thursday - the first time the trio of leaders have met together in person.

A full agenda has not been made public but there have been various hints about what could be discussed, including the wars in Ukraine and Iran, nuclear proliferation, trade tensions and developments in artificial intelligence.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin and Trump have not yet held a substantive meeting, and merely greeted each other on Wednesday.

Peskov also said that "no more than an hour" had been allocated for Thursday's trilateral talks between Putin, Trump and Xi.

national.title: Fiona the hippo undergoing care after swallowing a hat at Cincinnati Zoo
national.summary: Zookeepers say she cannot have surgery but are providing fluids and supportive care to help her pass the hat.
national.body:
The Cincinnati Zoo in Ohio says its beloved hippopotamus Fiona is undergoing emergency medical care after swallowing a knit hat that slipped into her enclosure.

The Zoo said that Fiona had swallowed the hat about nine days ago and was asymptomatic at first, adding that she was "large enough that a small-ish hat should be passing through".

But a few days later, her appetite started to decrease, and the zoo staff were trying to encourage Fiona to eat to help push the hat through her digestive system.

Fiona rose to fame when she was born premature at the Cincinnati Zoo and at first struggled to survive. Her story inspired an ice cream flavour as well as a character in Cincinnati's ballet.

Michelle Curley, a spokesperson for the zoo, told US media that the hat got into Fiona's enclosure by accident, after a visitor tossed it in the air and it caught on a ceiling fan that flung it through a small opening.

"We probably couldn't make [it] happen again if we tried," Curley said.

Zoo staff have been providing a series of supportive measures like fluids and ultrasounds to help Fiona recover.

The latest ultrasound showed the hat passing through Fiona's small intestine, the staff said, adding that she is still a bit dehydrated.

national.title: Bezos says he was "heavily involved" in casting Pattinson as 007
national.summary: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos says "it was obvious" to him and others that Robert Pattinson should be the next James Bond.
national.body: Amazon founder and executive chairman Jeff Bezos said Tuesday that he was "heavily involved" in casting Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond.Speaking at Semafor's Silicon Valley and The World forum in California, the head of the retail and entertainment giant that now owns the rights to the 007 franchise spoke about what he called the "real old-fashioned screen tests" for five Bond finalists, complete with "full costume, real sets."On Friday, the team of selectors spent several hours going over the screen tests of each actor, Bezos said in remarks reported by Semafor, adding that while they were all "extraordinarily talented … there was something special about Rob."Bezos said the group was initially biased against Pattinson, "because he's already so famous," and they had been inclined to choose someone "a little more unknown." The role of the iconic British spy has historically gone to lesser-known actors, who have then made their name doing the Bond movies. "But in the screening tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond," Bezos said of Pattinson, who shot to fame with his starring role in the "Twilight" vampire movies.Amazon bought MGM, which co-owns the rights to the Bond franchise, in 2022. Pattinson will be the first Bond not forged under the creative stewardship of the Broccoli family, who had run the franchise since 1962, when the first movie featuring 007, "Dr. No," was released."James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a statement after he was unveiled as the seventh actor to take on the role. "To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."He will step into the shoes of Hollywood leading men Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig to star in the 26th Bond movie, which will be directed by Denis Villeneuve. It is expected to hit screens in 2028.

national.title: Democrats formally nominate Hakeem Jeffries for speaker of the House
national.summary: The New York Democrat moved a step closer to becoming the first Black lawmaker in U.S. history to serve in the job, after House Democrats voted overwhelmingly to support him.
national.body:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has been nominated by House Democrats to serve as Speaker of the House when the party retakes the majority in the new year.

Wednesday's vote by House Democrats kickstarts the formal selection process for Speaker, which will take place at the start of the new Congress on January 3 with a vote on the floor of the House. If successful, as is widely expected, Jeffries will make history as the first Black lawmaker to serve in the job.

"Our message to the American people who are struggling in this failed economy is a simple one. We hear you, we see you, we feel you, and House Democrats are committed to making life better for you," Jeffries said after the vote.

Jeffries centered his remarks on cost of living issues, saying Democrats would fight to lower the cost of groceries, gas, housing and health care. And in the face of what he described as "unprecedented corruption," Jeffries said Democrats would work to hold officials accountable.

"Not for partisan reasons but for patriotic ones, because the American people deserve better," he said.

The New York Democrat ran uncontested, winning a closed-door vote by a tally of 251 to 11. His victory comes just over a week after House Republicans selected Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio to be the conference's minority leader; in the Senate, Republicans tapped South Dakota's John Thune for a second term as party leader.

Jeffries, who's led House Democrats since 2023, will need just a simple majority of member votes in a Congress where Democrats are poised to control at least 257 seats, with several remaining races still to be decided.

It's a vastly different reality from what awaited House Republicans four years ago when they regained the House majority. Facing extremely narrow margins, GOP leaders struggled to unite the conference around a speaker and were forced to negotiate with a handful of far-right party holdouts in order to reach consensus. After multiple candidates failed to secure a majority, the party ultimately coalesced around the now outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La.

national.title: Democrats nominate Hakeem Jeffries to become House speaker, a historic first
national.summary: Jeffries brushed past skeptics and was on track to make history as the nation's first Black American with the gavel.
national.body:
Lisa Mascaro, Associated Press Lisa Mascaro, Associated Press

WASHINGTON (AP) — Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries on Wednesday to be speaker of the House, as he brushed past skeptics and was on track to make history as the nation's first Black American with the gavel.

Jeffries, of New York, secured the nod during closed-door voting, ahead of a full House vote when the new Congress convenes in January.

He ran unopposed but faces a restive party eager for a change after voters ousted Republicans in a rebuke of President Donald Trump and the party in power. Phone calls and social media posts have been flooding the offices of Democrats and the newly elected, demanding a fresh start. Protesters heckled Jeffries last week during a Democratic conference in Denver.

Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News

Ahead of Wednesday's vote, Jeffries said he was taking nothing for granted. He met with the caucuses that make up the House Democrats and talked to almost all members in what will be their large majority.

Jeffries is part of a leadership trio with Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts and Rep. Pete Aguilar of California, who would all be historic firsts — Clark as the first female majority leader and Aguilar as the first Latino to serve as the majority whip. They also ran unopposed.

Jeffries will face a separate roll call of the whole House to become speaker when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3, 2027.

national.title: Woman describes confronting Rex Ryan after he allegedly hit her with truck
national.summary: Former New York Jets head coach Rex Ryan is facing several misdemeanor charges for allegedly striking a married couple with his truck.
national.body: Nadia Holland, who was allegedly hit by former NFL head coach Rex Ryan while he was driving in Nashville, Tennessee, told CBS News she's shocked there hasn't been more public outcry following the incident, saying it left her and her husband traumatized."Had we taken one more step, then I might have lost a leg," Holland told "CBS Mornings" in an exclusive interview.The former New York Jets and Buffalo Bills head coach faces six misdemeanor charges, including leaving the scene of an accident and failing to render aid. His bond was set at $6,000."He was at the next stoplight and he couldn't drive any farther because he was in traffic," Holland told "CBS Mornings." "So, we knocked on his window and said, 'Hey, you ran us over.' And so he comes out and starts screaming on the top of his lungs and doesn't want to hear it. When we tell him that we actually got run over by you, he gets in his truck and then drives off."Ryan, an ESPN analyst, returned to his job over the weekend, but did not address the allegations."Seeing him be on TV again and act like nothing has happened, this is not being taken serious enough because this shouldn't be happening," Holland said. "I can't cross the street now without looking twice, thinking what if something comes and strikes me again?""I'm just in shock, even today," she added.In 911 audio obtained by the New York Post, Nashville attorney Michael Holland described the moments he and his wife were allegedly struck by Ryan's pickup truck."My wife and I both got ran over by some a--hole on f---ing Broadway and I want to turn him in," Michael Holland is heard saying in the 911 audio."My toes are going to be a mess tomorrow," he said on the call, adding, "He f---ing needs to be arrested."Ryan surrendered to Nashville police on Nov. 11."I was looking at the license plate and my husband was like, 'It says New York Jets.' And so I'm not familiar with sports, but my husband said the next morning that this might be this guy," Nadia Holland said, referring to Ryan.Ryan's attorneys said he is cooperating with the investigation. They added he turned himself in to police when he learned about the charges and was released without having to post the $6,000 bond. ESPN said at the time it was aware of the incident and in touch with Ryan.He is scheduled to make his first court appearance on Dec. 18.Ryan has worked as an analyst for ESPN since 2017.

national.title: Inside China's race to get humanoid robot helpers into our homes
national.summary: China is racing to make humanoid robot helpers common home appliances, and one industry insider says they have an "edge globally."
national.body: Wuhan, China — In the large lobby of a three story building in Wuhan, China, a child-size yellow robot greets visitors with a dance. It sways along to traditional Chinese music while robots twice the size stand on either side of the stage, beating loud drums to the rhythm. The little robot then moves on to another dance, bopping along to a pop tune that makes people smile and laugh. The small humanoid robot's agility makes it look almost lifelike. Then it stops, and the crowd is ushered on to see the real wonders inside the Hubei Humanoid Robotics Innovation Center.On the top floor, more than 100 computer science and engineering graduates toil at individual work stations wearing gloves and outfits equipped with motion and tactile sensors, while cameras record their every movement.One pours water into a jug; another places cutlery and chopsticks into a container. The graduate at the next table unscrews a flashlight and removes the battery, then replaces it. All the movements are done slowly, meticulously and repeated over and over again, with the actions recorded as valuable data from the cameras and sensors that can be used to train the company's humanoid robots."It was fun at first," said 22-year-old intern Mei. "It gets a little boring in the middle. But it's such a proud moment when we get the model trained."Mei is one of nearly 1 million engineering graduates China's universities are estimated to be churning out every year. The U.S., by comparison, sends about 140,000 young engineers into the job market annually. Another graduate sits with a remote control in his hand and a humanoid robot next to him. As he moves his hand, the robot mimics his motions."Right now I'm capturing the motion of pouring water into a cup. We're training this action and gathering data for the model. It's controlled by this hand controller. It moves exactly how the hand moves," he explains. "We need to run this hundreds or thousands of times. national.title: Parents jailed for torture and death of four-year-old girl found along French motorway in 1987
national.summary: Inass Touloub's body was found along the A10 road in 1987, bearing marks of abuse, and was not identified until 2018.
national.body:
The mother of a four-year-old girl killed in central France and found along a motorway almost 40 years ago has been sentenced to 20 years in prison.

Halima El Bakhti, 72, was found guilty on Tuesday of "torture and acts of barbarity resulting in death without the intent to kill", French media reports.

The girl's father, 74-year-old Ahmed Touloub, was handed a 15-year sentence as an accomplice.

Four-year-old Inass Touloub was found along the A10 road in Suèvres in the Loir-et-Cher department on 11 August 1987. Her body bore multiple marks of abuse, including human bite marks, broken bones and burns with an iron.

She was buried in an unmarked grave near the location where her body was found. Unidentified for three decades, she was known only as the "Little Martyr of the A10".

Then, in 2018, she was identified after the DNA of her brother – tested in an unrelated case – matched with hers, leading to the arrest of their parents.

The trial took place in Loir-et-Cher Assize Court from 2 November, with the verdict delivered on Tuesday after several hours of deliberation.

During the trial, prosecutor Anaïs Allio emphasised that "not a single part of Inass's body was spared", and recalled the "sense of vertigo that overcame us all" upon viewing the "unbearable photographs" from the autopsy, France Info reports.

national.title: House Democrat warns 13 Trump allies to save their records for upcoming investigations
national.summary: Among the recipients of letters from Robert Garcia, incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, are Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump, Jared Kushner and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller.
national.body:
The highest-ranking Democrat on the House Oversight Committee sent document preservation letters to over a dozen of President Trump's allies and family members, laying the groundwork for incoming investigations come January.

"Oversight Democrats are fighting to put an end to this Administration's self-dealing, misconduct, and abuse," said Rep. Robert Garcia, who is poised to become the chair of the committee. "These investigations will lay the groundwork for legislation which helps all Americans. This is just the beginning."

The California Democrat's targets fall into four broad categories: "Trump family corruption, corporate corruption, DHS misconduct, and the White House Epstein cover-up."

"Americans should be secure in the knowledge that their government is focused on their best interests—not on making the President's family richer," many of the letters read.

The Trump administration has previously rejected accusations of misconduct and has warned Garcia that overly zealous investigations could constitute a crime — a claim legal experts have broadly pushed back against, citing Congress' oversight authorities.

In a letter dated Nov. 9, White House Counsel Will Scharf told Garcia the administration was "monitoring" the speech of Democrats in Congress as they mapped out investigative targets into the Trump administration. The letter warned that efforts by Democrats to investigate the administration "may cross the line into blatant criminality."

"As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement on Wednesday in response to Garcia's letters. "If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."

Canada's car industry has become one of the clearest stress tests for Ottawa as US tariffs threaten the sector.

"In my conversation with the president, he's tried to understand where we are with China, where we're going with China. I shouldn't speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it's not the top issue at all." Carney said prior to a meeting with Trump on the sidelines of the Apec summit.

The pair discussed discussed ongoing work towards a US-Canada trade agreement in their roughly 20 minute.

national.title: Nvidia says it will stop selling some data center chips to China
national.summary: Nvidia's sales to China are facing heightened scrutiny after revelations that former CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.
national.body: Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress said Tuesday that the company has stopped shipping artificial intelligence chips from its Hopper series to China, despite earlier U.S. approval to sell the technology there. The Hopper line, designed to speed training of AI models, includes the powerful H200 chip, which the U.S. Department of Commerce approved for sale in China in January. Kress didn't provide a reason for the decision, but the strategic shift comes amid heightened scrutiny of Nvidia's sales in China following revelations that former CEO and cofounder Jensen Huang had a relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Huang, who successfully lobbied the Trump administration to ease export controls on its advanced chips, had agreed to give the U.S. government 15% of revenue generated by sales of its AI chips in China. Kress said that sales of licensed Hopper products to China totaled $2.4 billion in the third quarter, or about 2% of its total revenue. But "our guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included, and we are no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China," she said in a call with Wall Street analysts to discuss Nvidia's latest financial results. Dilin Wu, a research strategist at Pepperstone, told Agence France-Presse that "the timing says quite a lot.""We don't know exactly what prompted the decision to stop shipments, but it certainly looks like Nvidia is trying to draw a clearer line around its China business and reassure regulators that compliance comes first," Wu said.Nvidia also said on Tuesday that its board has formed a panel to oversee its national security policies and compliance with U.S. export controls. Washington still bans exports of Nvidia's more advanced Blackwell and Rubin GPUs to China, citing security concerns over AI's use in military applications.Nvidia reported robust growth as Kress hosted her first earnings call since Huang resigned last week after it emerged that he had at least extramarital affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. authorities have linked to Chinese intelligence and a direct subordinate at Nvidia. The chipmaker reported fiscal third-quarter profits of $65.3 billion, topping analyst forecasts and up 105% from earnings of $31.9 billion in the year-ago period. Nvidia's revenue rose to $115.8 billion, compared with $57 billion a year ago.

Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at between $70 - $78 each.

If they go for the highest price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $18.5bn each.

So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy?

In 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT.

He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him.

Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track , and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity.

Kuwait and Bahrain have said they repelled Iranian air attacks overnight as hostilities between Iran and the United States rise.

The drone attack on Kuwait was the first in more than two months. The Iranian army said it had targeted the Ali Al Salem Airbase, which hosts US forces, but Kuwaiti authorities did not report any damage.

It came after US warplanes struck an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, according to US military officials.

Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates' state oil firm said a crew member was missing after one of its tankers was attacked in the Gulf waterway on Tuesday.

The recent exchanges of fire, as well as deadlock in negotiations on a peace deal, have raised fears of a major escalation in the nine-month-old war.

It has also attacked dozens of commercial vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass.

national.title: The off-and-on switch for U.S. aid leads to a cliffhanger for Zambia and Zimbabwe
national.summary: After dismantling the United States Agency for International Development, the Trump administration is restarting foreign aid. In Zambia and Zimbabwe, there are different approaches but similar worries.
national.body:
Rahul Mukherjee/NPR This is a story that starts with a remarkable success story. However, the ending has become a cliff hanger — with potentially grave consequences.

The success is clearcut and remarkable: Both Zambia and Zimbabwe are beating back devastating HIV/AIDS epidemics. These neighboring countries in southern Africa are on the cusp of controlling the virus.

Between 2000 and 2025, new infections dropped by 76% in Zambia and 80% in Zimbabwe. In both countries, more than 95% of infected individuals are identified and 95% of them are on treatment, according to data from the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS.

This progress is thanks, in large part, to billions of dollars in U.S. aid over the past two decades.

However, President Trump's new global health strategy is scrambling the landscape. After dismantling without warning the U.S. Agency for International Development in 2025, the administration is now hammering out government-to-government aid agreements as a new framework for how aid is provided.

That process leaves these two countries on very different paths and heading toward uncharted territory.

Just last month Zambian and U.S. officials signed an agreement — albeit for far less annual U.S. health aid than the country received in the past. Zimbabwe, in contrast, lost all U.S. health aid this fall after negotiations collapsed. To get an on-the-ground assessment of what has happened and what the future may hold, NPR interviewed a health worker in each country with experience in the HIV/AIDS world.

When the aid agreement was announced on ZNBC — Zambia National Broadcasting Corporation on October 8 — it was branded as "a new chapter" in which the U.S. aid dollars flow primarily through the government and aims to build up the national health system.

local.title: The construction of High Falls State Park has begun
local.summary: The groundbreaking of the park took place on Wednesday, with the first phase focusing on the eastern rim of High Falls gorge.
local.body:
The ground has been broken on what will be the first state park in the city of Rochester.

High Falls State Park will span 85 acres in and around the High Falls gorge and will feature a mix of trails, playgrounds, overlooks, and pavilions. The first phase of the park will focus on the Heritage Walk on the eastern edge of the gorge, at the site of the former High Falls Terrace Park. That site will pay homage to the various cultures that make up Rochester's heritage, from the Haudenosaunee to Irish immigrants.

"This is really a whole new chapter for Rochester," Gov. Kathy Hochul said during a ceremony Wednesday. "For generations, Rochester families have had to live alongside the Genesee River. They've heard the water, they've seen the gorge...they can proudly say that one of the most spectacular natural wonders in New York State, right here behind me, High Falls, 80 feet of waterfalls in the middle of downtown, is now available for the public."

Hochul included $300 million towards development projects in Rochester in her budget for this fiscal year. Of that, $75 million was earmarked for the park's development.

The park was long used as a site for Rochester Gas and Electric and other industrial purposes. A cleanup project in the gorge is still underway.

"Where we are today is transformational," Mayor Malik Evans said. "I think it's hard for you all to really contemplate how transformational and how much of a big deal it is."

The completed park is expected to be finished over the next four years.

local.summary: The Dunkirk Common Council advanced a law that would override a state-imposed property tax cap. Rhetoric about the proposed 2027 city budget dominated the council meeting. Passing the tax cap law would directly affect the budget, allowing City Hall to soak Dunkirk property owners for more money. May
local.body:
The Dunkirk Common Council advanced a law that would override a state-imposed property tax cap.

Rhetoric about the proposed 2027 city budget dominated the council meeting. Passing the tax cap law would directly affect the budget, allowing City Hall to soak Dunkirk property owners for more money. Mayor Kate Wdowiasz's proposed 2027 budget calls for an approximately 11% tax increase.

Council voted 4-1 to schedule a public hearing on the law before its next meeting on Dec. 1. Councilwoman Natalie Luczkowiak voted "no."

Prior to the tax cap hearing vote, council members offered extensive comments on the proposed law and 2027 budget. Luczkowiak went first, explaining why she would vote against the tax cap override.

"This is not a vote on whether we have financial problems -- we do. This is a vote on whether we have earned the right to ask taxpayers to pay more than the state allows -- we have not," she said.

Luczkowiak noted the gigantic 86% tax increase from two years ago. "That was sold to the public as a fix. It was supposed to stabilize our finances -- it did not."

She said the override option "is meant to be a last resort after a municipality has cut spending, used reserves, shared services, and proven it has no other choice. The council has not been shown that work."

Instead, "What we are being asked to do is use a permanent tax increase to pay for ongoing structural deficits."

local.body:
SUNY Fredonia is not sharing in the enrollment gains happening throughout much of the SUNY system, including Jamestown Community College.

Some grim news was buried in a breezy SUNY press release Wednesday that touted a nearly 8% enrollment increase across the system since 2022.

SUNY Fredonia’s overall enrollment is down 17.5% since fall 2021. Its rate for first-time undergraduates is even worse over the same period: Down 26.1%. That figure is the worst among SUNY’s state-run universities, a group that excludes community colleges like JCC.

Fredonia’s enrollment is down 2.2% from last fall. The overall SUNY rate shows an increase of 1.3% since 2025.

JCC’s numbers look better. While its overall enrollment rate is down 2.9% from fall 2025, it has actually gone up 1.1% since fall 2021.

The enrollment rate for first time undergraduates at JCC is showing solid gains. It's up 10.8% since fall 2025 and 19.2% since fall 2021.

The bad SUNY Fredonia news is not really new -- it's a reframing of some figures known for a while.

SUNY Fredonia's student body "head count" was 3,108 students on Sept. 21, enrollment vice president Kathryn Kendall reported at the first University Council meeting of the 2026-27 school year.

local.body:
Dear Annie: I recently met a wonderful woman while on vacation, and what started as a casual conversation turned into something neither of us expected. We spent several days together, laughing, talking for hours and feeling a connection that seemed almost too good to be true. There was chemistry, but there was also something deeper. We talked about our families, our lives and even the possibility of seeing each other again.

When we returned home, the connection continued. We texted throughout the day, exchanged good morning and good night messages, and shared little details about our lives. She seemed just as interested as I was. Sometimes she even initiated the conversations. I found myself looking forward to hearing from her, and I began to believe this might actually turn into something meaningful.

local.title: Who benefits from High Falls State Park might depend on what happens next
local.summary: "This park is transformational for downtown Rochester," said Lisa Baron, executive chairperson of the nonprofit Greentopia. "But we want it transformational for everybody."
local.body:
With the start of construction on High Falls State Park comes a challenge to ensure the millions to be invested creates not just a regional attraction but a community benefit.

"This park is transformational for downtown Rochester," said Lisa Baron, executive chairperson of the nonprofit Greentopia . "But we want it transformational for everybody."

The park will encompass 40 acres, mostly in the Genesee River gorge extending north from the flume, and Greentopia is on track to become a "friends of" supporting organization, helping with programming, workforce training and other needs.

New York has committed $75 million for planning and construction, but more money will be needed. Initial park development will start up on the east ridge of the gorge, at Falls Terrace Park off St. Paul Street.

"And the plans over there are quite dramatic, right?" Baron said. "There'll actually be an overlook where you can see the falls that's not obscured by trees. You'll have public restrooms, which are critical. There'll be, you know, picnic tables and meeting spaces, and it'll be a real introduction to what the future park could look like."

The park will be built in phases, and is expected to take years to complete. But lessons from elsewhere show the time for planning on what is to come beyond the park boundaries is now.

"We have a chance to really set in motion all of the outreach and the mechanisms that'll make it possible so that everybody benefits," Baron said, adding: "We don't want the gentrification that happened with the High Line to happen here."

The elevated High Line park in New York City is a case study in eco-gentrification . Property values shot up. So did population in the surrounding neighborhoods, with an influx of higher-income residents. The mix of neighborhood business flipped from auto repair, meat packing and print shops to galleries, tech offices and specialty retail.

local.body:
The CHQ Chamber is pleased to announce Michael Edwards, Director of the Jamestown Renaissance Corporation, as the keynote speaker for its 2026 Annual Meeting on Friday, Dec. 11, at the Chautauqua Harbor Hotel.

Edwards will share his experience and insights on downtown revitalization and economic development, drawing from his work in communities including Chicago, Pittsburgh, Spokane, and Jamestown. His presentation will explore the importance of creating vibrant downtown districts, supporting local businesses, attracting investment, and building places where people want to live, work, shop, and connect.

As Director of the Jamestown Renaissance Corporation, Edwards leads downtown revitalization efforts focused on organization, design and rehabilitation, economic and business development, and marketing.

Previously, Edwards served as President and CEO of Chicago Loop Alliance for 13 years, where he led initiatives to strengthen the downtown experience through strategic planning, business development, placemaking, public space activation, events, and advocacy. He also held leadership roles with the Pittsburgh Downtown Partnership and Downtown Spokane Partnership and served as a principal with The Saratoga Associates, a New York-based urban planning consulting firm.

A recognized expert in downtown management, Edwards is a founding member of the Global Business District Innovation Club, a Senior Fellow of the Institute of Place Management, and a past member of the International Downtown Association Board of Directors. He frequently speaks internationally about the opportunities and challenges facing downtown districts. As the holiday season encourages shoppers to explore and support local businesses, Edwards’ perspective offers a timely look at the connections between vibrant downtowns and thriving business communities.

"Strong downtowns and thriving local businesses go hand in hand," said Daniel Heitzenrater, CHQ Chamber President & CEO. "Michael brings a wealth of experience and a valuable perspective on how communities can create welcoming, engaging downtown experiences that encourage people to shop local, support businesses, and build connections. We look forward to hearing his insights and how they can help inform the continued growth of our communities throughout Chautauqua County."

The Annual Meeting will feature breakfast, networking, updates from the CHQ Chamber, the election of board members, and presentation of the Pam Lydic Coalition Builder Award, in addition to Edwards' keynote presentation. The event will take place at 8 a.m. Tickets are $40 for CHQ Chamber members and $45 for non-members. Registration is available on the Chamber's online calendar at: chqchamber.org. local.body:
Submitted Photo Jess, shown here, is a 7-year-old Labrador retriever who loves to hunt with his master and best friend, local author John Jarzynski. It was a good day in the field this week for both of them, with a two-bird daily pheasant limit (one hen, one cock) taken on public land in Western New York.

NYSDEC Illustration For the 2026-27 season, the DEC pheasant hunting map identifies cock-and-hen hunting areas with an Oct. 17 opener that will generally remain open through Feb. 28, while designated cock-only areas close Dec. 31.

When New York’s Southern Zone early archery season gets underway, much of the attention turns to whitetail deer and black bear. But there’s another hunting tradition unfolding across Western New York’s fields and grasslands, one that sometimes gets overlooked: pheasant hunting.

For John Jarzynski, a Western New York outdoorsman and book author (look him up), it’s a season he looks forward to every year. He doesn’t go alone.

His hunting companion is a 7-year-old whose technical name is Marshfield Jessie’s Gift JH, better known as Jess. The JH designation represents her American Kennel Club Junior Hunter title, an achievement that reflects her natural ability and training.

Jess loves birds. Ducks, pheasants and geese all get her attention. While Jarzynski’s kennel is filled with beagles waiting for rabbit season, he spends much of September through November taking Jess afield.

He has hunted snow geese with her in North Dakota, but some of his favorite memories are made much closer to home.

"I've written about my life of just watching her in the field, the way she scans the skies for ducks, or how her body trembles when she smells a pheasant. It's 90% of why I hunt. The dog is being purposeful. Truth is, she takes me hunting," Jarzynski said.

local.title: ‘Exciting opportunity’
local.summary: Two area girls with family histories of success at the pool will be taking their talents to the New York State Public High School Athletic Association Swimming & Diving Championships this weekend. Anelia Pitts of Frewsburg and Clarissa Hren of Southwestern earned a trip to the Webster Aquatic Center
local.body:
Two area girls with family histories of success at the pool will be taking their talents to the New York State Public High School Athletic Association Swimming & Diving Championships this weekend.

Anelia Pitts of Frewsburg and Clarissa Hren of Southwestern earned a trip to the Webster Aquatic Center by virtue of their respective performances in 1-meter diving and the 200-yard individual medley at the state qualifier earlier this month.

A junior, Pitts finished in second place at Erie Community College's Burt Flickinger Athletic Center with a cumulative score of 484.35 to break Frewsburg's record of 475.3 previously held by her sister, Elayna.

"I feel very honored to get to go," Pitts said Monday night during a break in a workout at the Jamestown Community College pool. "It's really rewarding. There's been a lot of work put in this season. I had a lot of help from my primary coach, Scott Scholeno, and also from John Crawford and the coaches at Buffalo Blizzards (Diving Club)."

Meanwhile, Hren, a senior, placed second in the 200-yard individual medley at the state qualifier with a time of 2:15.37 to punch her ticket to suburban Rochester.

"To me, it's such a big deal, because this is all I've been working towards for 13 years of swimming," Hren said.

Pitts, who will be returning to the state meet for the second straight year, is following the diving path blazed by her older siblings, Xander and Elayna.

"She's been following in her brother's and sister's shadow forever," Scholeno said, "and she finally broke free from that. I'm just proud of her. ... She's the best we've had."

local.body:
OBSERVER File Photo Ellicottville/Franklinville senior Tosh Klein was named the CCAA DII Player of the Year.

The Ellicottville/Franklinville boys soccer team went undefeated en route to claiming the Chautauqua-Cattaraugus Athletic Association Division II championship and the Eagles did it with three of the top five players in the league.

Senior Tosh Klein was named the Player of the Year after scoring a whopping 25 goals and 20 assists, contributing to 56% of the goals scored by the eventual Section VI Class C champions. Senior Coleman Carls was named the Defensive Player of the Year, scoring six goals and six assists, and the Eagles defense posted five clean sheets in league play to go along with a plus-59 goal differential this season.

Along with the individual honors, the entire coaching staff was named for the Coach of the Year award.

Joining his Eagles teammates in the Top 5 players in the league as the No. 3 overall player was junior Holden Basher, who scored 22 goals and 16 assists.

Klein and Basher were named to the league's First Team at forward; Carls was joined in the midfield by senior Teddy Edwards, who posted four goals and five assists; and senior Timmy DeChane earned a spot on the defense while scoring two goals.

Ellicottville/Franklinville also had junior Rian Johnson named to the Second Team at midfield and junior Liem Haynoski joined him on the defense.

Portville was the only team to have a decision other than a loss against Ellicottville/Franklinville when it tied the Eagles in the first meeting of the season. Leading the Panthers in that performance and all season long was senior Colin German, who was named the league's Offensive Player of the Year after scoring 15 goals and 12 assists while being named the second-best player.

local.title: The OBSERVER’s View: Drayo’s history, knowledge a community gift
local.summary: For many lifelong residents of northern Chautauqua County, Sam Drayo Jr. was synonymous with Fredonia. He served as the village’s municipal attorney for 47 years and took pride in remembering those who came before him and helped build the community’s legacy. To Drayo, that history always mattered. H
local.body:
For many lifelong residents of northern Chautauqua County, Sam Drayo Jr. was synonymous with Fredonia. He served as the village's municipal attorney for 47 years and took pride in remembering those who came before him and helped build the community's legacy.

His knowledge and passion will be missed throughout this corner of the county. Over the years, he shared many lessons with us, offering a wealth of historical information and personal recollections.

Only days before his death, one of his articles was published in our Veterans Day section on Nov. 7. It was headlined "Honoring Those Connected to a Church and All Who Served."

The article was especially meaningful and emotional for Drayo because it included information about his cousin, Richard Drayo. Here is an excerpt from that essay:

"There were many veterans from the Dunkirk-Fredonia area who selflessly and honorably served their country in World War II. These young Americans underwent great sacrifices for our country. Many of them spending 2-4 years away from home with no means of communication with their loved ones at home, other than an occasional letter. No cell phones or email existed in those days. They endured much hardship. For their sacrifices, hard work ethic and contributions to our country, they are now rightfully referred to as 'The Greatest Generation.'

"From the small Parish of St. Anthony's Roman Catholic Church in Fredonia, 168 young first generation Americans honorably served their country in World War II. In 1945, the Bishop of the Buffalo Diocese, John F. O'Hara, wrote a letter to the Rev. Pio Parolin, the longest serving pastor of St. Anthony's Church (1934 to 1953) stating, 'My congratulations to the men and women of St. Anthony's Parish who are serving their country all over the world.'"

Drayo's recollections, many of which were published in the OBSERVER, were a gift to this community. His dedication to preserving local history ensured that stories of the people and events that shaped this area would not be forgotten.

Family and friends are invited to call from 3 to 7 p.m. today at the LARSON-TIMKO Funeral Home, 20 Central Ave., Fredonia.

local.title: Six Buffalo firefighters injured while rescuing victims from Scoville Avenue fire
local.summary: Six Buffalo firefighters were injured and an 11-year-old girl was rescued from the second floor of a burning home after a Mayday was called during a fierce fire on Scoville Avenue Monday afternoon.
local.body: Six Buffalo firefighters were injured and an 11-year-old girl was rescued from the second floor of a burning home after a Mayday was called during a fierce fire on Scoville Avenue Monday afternoon.The fire broke out at 138 Scoville Ave. at about 3:30 p.m., where firefighters arrived to find heavy flames and reports that people could be trapped inside.“We have children and adults jumping out the front window,” a firefighter could be heard saying over the radio.With reports of people still inside, firefighters entered the home. During the response, a Mayday was called after firefighters became trapped on the second floor.“We're by an open window. We don't know which side,” one firefighter could be heard saying over the radio.Other firefighters worked to locate the trapped crew as conditions deteriorated.“Gotta get a ladder up here,” a firefighter said.WATCH: Six Buffalo firefighters injured while rescuing victims from Scoville Avenue fireEventually, a trapped firefighter was located and brought to safety, prompting the Mayday to be cleared.“Firefighter is confirmed out. Disregard the Mayday,” the radio transmission said.Crews then reported bringing another victim out from the second floor and requested additional ambulances because of multiple victims.Buffalo Fire Commissioner Daniel Pizarro said firefighters were dealing simultaneously with the Mayday and reports that people remained trapped inside the burning home.Pizarro said crews briefly lost their water supply during the fire.“Within those few seconds, the fire was intense enough to trap those firemen,” Pizarro said.Amid the chaos, firefighters rescued an 11-year-old girl from the second floor. She was taken to the hospital for treatment.Six firefighters were also injured. Pizarro said their injuries included second-degree burns to the head, lacerations, eye injuries, twisted backs and smoke inhalation.All six have since been released from the hospital and are recovering, according to Pizarro.“My firemen, I'm very proud of you, Buffalo Fire,” Pizarro said. “You did what you do every day, and I'm proud to represent this department, and we will continue to protect the city in whatever situation comes our way.”7 News will continue to follow the condition of the 11-year-old girl.

local.summary: Former acting Mayor Christopher Scanlon says there wasn't money to schedule a police recruitment exam as Buffalo's police staffing problems get worse.
local.body: Former acting Buffalo Mayor Christopher Scanlon says the city did not schedule a police recruitment exam during his tenure because it lacked the money to fund one. It's a decision that comes into focus as the Buffalo Police Department faces mounting staffing problems.BPD representatives and the police union appeared before the Common Council to discuss the recruitment vacuum, Tuesday. The next police exam is scheduled for the end of April 2027 which means a fresh class of officers will not be on the streets of Buffalo until some point in 2028 at the earliest. The last time the city administered a police exam to try to recruit officers was in 2023 and Police Commissioner Erika Shields previously blamed the subsequent three-year pause for the department's staffing woes.The city's Human Resources Commissioner, Gladys Herndon-Hill echoed that claim in the meeting.
